timelineEvents.title: Earliest documented compositions for film
timelineEvents.label: 1930 · Earliest film compositions
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Kaper’s earliest documented work for the cinema is music for three German sound films of 1930.
timelineEvents.longDescription: Music for Die lustigen Musikanten, directed by Max Obal, Alraune, directed by Richard Oswald, and Der Korvettenkapitän, directed by Rudolf Walther-Fein, all released in 1930. For Alraune Kaper wrote two tangos to words by Fritz Rotter, “Nur Tango, nur Tango” and “Wenn mich Männer betrügen”; Der Korvettenkapitän carried four of his songs, again to Rotter’s words.

timelineEvents.title: Migration from Berlin via Vienna to Paris
timelineEvents.label: 1933 · Berlin–Vienna–Paris migration
timelineEvents.shortDescription: After Nazi persecution intensifies, Kaper and Jurmann leave Berlin and relocate toward Paris.
timelineEvents.longDescription: In 1933, after UFA terminated the contracts of its Jewish employees, Kaper and Jurmann left Berlin and, by way of Vienna, settled in Paris. His route ran through Vienna, where he had supervised the French version of Abenteuer am Lido, and the departure itself falls between the spring and the summer of 1933. Kaper’s oral history returns twice to an attack on him and his wife by a group of Nazis in a Berlin street, once within a story about self-defence and once as an aside to his account of film work, where he set it apart from his music. The attack does not explain his music, but it marks the point at which working conditions in the German film industry could no longer be separated from questions of safety.

timelineEvents.title: Paris period
timelineEvents.label: 1933–1934 · Paris period
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Kaper works in Paris for French producers, contributing songs and film music with Jurmann.
timelineEvents.longDescription: About eighteen months of work for French producers. Matthias Brzoska describes Paris for the duo as less a place of exile than a career stage: in the 1933/34 season their revues dominated the Folies Bergère and the Casino de Paris, and they wrote for the Casino revue Parade de France. Besides French versions of earlier German films, Kaper and Jurmann supplied the music for Une femme au volant, On a volé un homme, Le Greluchon délicat and Les Nuits moscovites, with hits including “Natacha” and “On n’aime qu’une fois”. Jacques Ibert praised the Nuits moscovites score in Le Matin as never intrusive and always suited to its subject. The Paris address Kaper gave on arrival in New York was the Château Frontenac hotel at 54 rue Pierre Charron.

timelineEvents.title: European afterlife
timelineEvents.label: 1934–1936 · European afterlife
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Jurmann–Kaper films and songs continue circulating in Europe after the composers leave for America.
timelineEvents.longDescription: While the composers head to America, their European films and songs continue to circulate. In September 1934, “Madame wird kinderlieb” still plays in Stuttgart with Jurmann and Kaper credited — despite Nazi purges. In France, “Tout pour l’amour” with Kiepura screens as late as 1936; the Journal de Vichy calls their music “infiniment plaisante.” The inconsistency of the exclusion is visible earlier still: on 25 August 1933 the Westfälische Zeitung advertised Madame wird kinderlieb with the credit “Musik von Jurmann und Kaper” on the same page as an advertisement for a racist handbook of German ethnology.

timelineEvents.title: Arrival in New York en route to Los Angeles
timelineEvents.label: 24 Oct 1934 · Arrival in New York
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Kaper arrives in New York from France with Eleonora, holding a temporary visa and travelling onward to Los Angeles.
timelineEvents.longDescription: Kaper and his wife Eleonora sailed from Le Havre on 17 October 1934 aboard the S.S. Champlain in second cabin class and reached New York on 24 October. Their non-immigrant visas had been issued in Paris on 15 October, numbered in a single series with the Jurmanns’ (NI 1581–1584), and the manifest records Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer as having paid the passage and as the party they were joining in Culver City. Kaper gave his occupation as musician and declared that he meant to stay about eight months and then return, without seeking United States citizenship. David Blum of the Culver Export Corporation met them in New York, and they left for Hollywood on 27 October.

timelineEvents.title: Legal Permanent Entry
timelineEvents.label: 1 Nov 1935 · Permanent U.S. entry
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Kaper enters the United States for permanent residence through Calexico with Eleonora.
timelineEvents.longDescription: Enters for permanent residence at Calexico, California, from Mexicali on 1 November 1935, travelling on foot with Eleonora. The manifest records 6626 Franklin Ave., Hollywood, as his U.S. destination; his Declaration of Intention four months later records the same address as his residence. The crossing followed the Immigration and Naturalization Service pre-examination procedure: Kaper gave the Commercial Hotel in Mexicali as his last permanent residence abroad and entered on a consular immigration visa, C.I.V. no. 1/24, issued there under Section 5 of the Immigration Act of 1924 and charged to the Polish quota. The manifest records his previous stay in California from 24 October 1934 to 20 October 1935, and his Polish passport no. 10568, issued by the Consulate General in Paris on 5 August 1934 and expired on 25 August 1935.

timelineEvents.title: Hollywood debut
timelineEvents.label: 1935 · Hollywood debut
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Kaper makes his Hollywood debut at MGM, contributing to Escapade and other major studio projects.
timelineEvents.longDescription: The first American score documented here is “Escapade” (dir. Robert Z. Leonard) with William Powell and Luise Rainer. Press hails “Two New Composers” of Kiepura’s European hits. Songs also for Marx Brothers’ “A Night at the Opera” (with Ned Washington) and “Mutiny on the Bounty”. MGM engaged Kaper at first as a song specialist rather than as a film composer, and by his own account he moved only gradually from songwriter to composer of scores. For Escapade, which opened in July 1935, he supplied a single number, “You’re All I Need”, to words by Gus Kahn.

timelineEvents.title: San Francisco success and Three Smart Girls
timelineEvents.label: 1936 · San Francisco and Three Smart Girls
timelineEvents.shortDescription: The title song from San Francisco becomes a major hit, while Kaper and Jurmann also contribute to Universal’s Three Smart Girls.
timelineEvents.longDescription: The success of San Francisco made Kaper and Jurmann more visible in Hollywood and helped establish Kaper’s reputation beyond the MGM studio system. The event also includes Three Smart Girls, the Universal production associated with Deanna Durbin and Joseph Pasternak. Tommy Dorsey’s recording of the title song stood third in the Victor column of The Billboard’s ten best records for the week ended 3 August 1936.

timelineEvents.title: Declarations of Intention
timelineEvents.label: 4 Feb 1936 · Declarations of Intention
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Bronisław and Eleonora Kaper file Declarations of Intention to become U.S. citizens in Los Angeles.
timelineEvents.longDescription: On 4 February 1936, Bronisław Kaper and Eleonora Kaper each filed a Declaration of Intention in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of California, Los Angeles. Bronisław Kaper’s declaration records him as residing at Château des Fleurs, 6626 Franklin Ave., Hollywood. A Certificate of Arrival issued on 2 January 1936 had confirmed the Calexico entry, in a document valid, as its own form states, for naturalisation purposes only; its number, 23-46078, recurs on the declaration and ties the two documents together.

timelineEvents.title: The Sängerfilm and the star-singer circuit
timelineEvents.label: Sängerfilm circuit
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Kaper and Jurmann’s songs entered the Sängerfilm economy, where screen performance, star singers, sheet music, records, radio, and dance-band repertory reinforced one another.
timelineEvents.longDescription: The Kaper–Jurmann partnership developed inside the commercial ecology of early European musical film. Their songs for productions associated with singers such as Richard Tauber and Jan Kiepura were not simply film numbers: they were designed to travel beyond the screen as printed music, recordings, radio items, and repertory for performers. This star-singer circuit explains why the duo’s European experience later appeared useful to MGM, which read it through the promotional language of Viennese musical competence.

timelineEvents.title: Multiple-language versions and transnational sound-film production
timelineEvents.label: Transnational sound film
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Before 1933, Kaper and Jurmann were already working within the multiple-language version system that linked Babelsberg, Joinville, Vienna, and other European production centres.
timelineEvents.longDescription: The practice of producing parallel language versions was one of the key industrial conditions of early sound cinema. It allowed music to move more easily than dialogue across national markets, even when lyrics, singers, and performance contexts changed. Kaper and Jurmann’s work in this system gave their songs and professional skills a transnational character before their forced departure from Germany.

timelineEvents.title: Ninon reaches Louis B. Mayer: the Ritz meeting and MGM contract
timelineEvents.label: Ninon opens the MGM path
timelineEvents.shortDescription: The European success of Ninon reportedly brought Kaper and Jurmann to the attention of Louis B. Mayer, leading to a meeting at the Hôtel Ritz and an MGM contract.
timelineEvents.longDescription: Kaper later recalled that the success of Ninon—written for Tout pour l’amour, the French version of Ein Lied für Dich—was the turning point that opened the path to Hollywood. Louis B. Mayer reached Paris on 7 August 1934, on a European trip that combined business with the search for new talent, and reportedly asked to meet the song’s authors, heard them perform at the Hôtel Ritz, and offered a seven-year MGM contract.

timelineEvents.title: MGM markets Kaper and Jurmann as “Viennese composers”
timelineEvents.label: MGM’s “Viennese” label
timelineEvents.shortDescription: American studio publicity recast Kaper and Jurmann as a Viennese composing team, turning “Vienna” into a promotional brand rather than a biographical fact.
timelineEvents.longDescription: Soon after their arrival at MGM, the American press and studio publicity presented Kaper and Jurmann as “Viennese composers”. The label suited MGM’s first use of the duo in Escapade, a Hollywood remake of the Viennese film Maskerade, but it was biographically misleading for Kaper, whose career had developed in Warsaw and Berlin. The event marks the moment when Hollywood began to translate his European professional history into a marketable studio identity. The label outlasted their arrival: in December 1936 the Viennese paper Telegraf itself wrote of “die Wiener Komponisten Kaper und Jurmann”.

places.authorizedName: French Line Pier 57, North River, foot of West 15th Street, Manhattan, New York
places.publicNote: Approximate arrival site for Kaper and Eleonora’s 1934 Atlantic crossing from Le Havre aboard the S.S. Champlain. In this period the French Line (Compagnie Générale Transatlantique) used Pier 57 on the North River, at the foot of West 15th Street; the pier is inferred from the line’s documented berth rather than named in the passenger manifest. The record establishes arrival at New York but not processing at Ellis Island.

French port city context for Kaper’s 1934 Atlantic crossing from Le Havre to New York aboard the S.S. Champlain. The marker is placed at city level: in 1934 CGT liners still used the port’s earlier transatlantic quays, since the landmark Gare Maritime on the quai Johannès-Couvert opened only in May 1935 (with the Normandie) and was destroyed in the 1944 bombing of Le Havre.

Vienna functions here as a European music-film and publicity context for the Berlin–Paris–Hollywood route and the star-singer circuit. MGM’s later “Viennese composers” label is not presented as Kaper’s biographical origin.

Major German film-production centre associated with the multiple-language version system in early European sound cinema. The marker represents the broader historic Babelsberg studio complex; no individual stage or production building is asserted for the linked context.
French studio/production-centre context for early sound-film multiple-language version production.

West Berlin district context for Kaper’s settled Berlin position before the 1933 forced departure. His address is identified as Pommersche Straße in Wilmersdorf, an affluent western Berlin residential district.

Documented Berlin residence: the Berliner Adreßbuch 1932 lists B. Kaper, composer, at Pommersche Straße 3 in Wilmersdorf. A later official planning record identifies the historical corner parcel as Sächsische Straße 48–49 / Pommersche Straße 3–4. Numbers 3–4 are absent from the present official address register, so the marker locates the historical corner parcel approximately rather than a surviving entrance.
